title: How to build a knowledge factory for AI agents
summary: The knowledge factory is how LangChain keeps its agents' company knowledge current: agents flag what's missing, and a curator agent fixes it in the background.
story_key: story|title:how to build a knowledge factory for ai agents
content_excerpt: In order to make AI work for your company, the missing bit is not better models, it’s not just more context - it’s better knowledge. It’s knowledge of how your company works, what standards for operating you have in place, where data is stored and how it’s accessed. Your most efficient employees have this knowledge in their head. They know who to talk to, where to go to answer questions, why you do things in a particular way. That knowledge is often tacit, implicit, scattered - sometimes present only in their head, sometimes scattered across a variety of documents. In order to make AI work for your company, you need to collect, curate, and maintain a representation of that knowledge to pass to agents. The system that helps you do that is what we’re calling a knowledge factory. We’ve built this at LangChain in a few ways. Our internal GTM and content studio agents are powered by a knowledge factory. LangSmith Engine (our agent that runs over traces and suggests fixes) maintains a knowledge factory per agent as well. This blog shares our learnings. Knowledge is the reusable understanding we maintain so it can do that task correctly: what a metric means, which source to trust, or how we handle a particular situation. Sometimes written down, often not. A knowledge factory turns scattered documents and experience into knowledge that can become context for future work. So knowledge is a form of context that the agent will get, but it’s often not (and shouldn’t be) the only context the agent gets. Other types of context you already ingest/store reliably, and that can just be provided directly to the agent (see the section on quickly changing data below). The idea of software factories has risen sharply over the past year and a half. The idea is that rather than having your best engineers actually build software, they should build the factory (the systems) to help everyone at the company build software more efficiently. The actual building of the software can be done by agents. General knowledge work is now following a similar path. Agents are good enough to make presentations, launch videos, do outbound. You should be leveraging them as much as possible for those tasks. But in order for them to accomplish those tasks they need all that tacit, implicit, scattered knowledge. title: Xing-Audio-NVVASR: Scaling and Refining Supervision for Joint Recognition of Speech and Non-Verbal Vocalizations
summary: Joint recognition of speech and non-verbal vocalizations (NVVs) is hindered by scarce event-rich training data and inaccurate or missing event labels. We present Xing-Audio-NVVASR, an end-to-end recognizer trained through progressive data mining and iterative supervision refinement. Guided by unified acoustic criteria, two heterogeneous models cross-audit annotations, flagging disagreements for teacher reannotation. To uncover shared omissions that model agreement may conceal, complementary breath detectors screen the entire corpus for human review. Human-confirmed labels accumulate across rounds and are preserved during subsequent refinement. Over five rounds, we refine annotations for 170,000 utterances from public corpora and incorporate 630,000 mined utterances. The resulting corpus of approximately 800,000 utterances is used to train a single 1.7B-parameter model that transcribes speech with inline tags for six NVV classes. Across four human-annotated benchmarks, Xing-Audio-NVVASR ranks first among nine models in both composite score and six-class Macro-F1. It achieves a mean composite score of 64.46, surpassing the strongest comparison model, StepAudio 3 Chat Preview, by 6.03 points, and exceeds the annotation teacher's breathing F1 by 14.40 to 31.57 percentage points. We plan to release the model weights, inference code, four evaluation benchmarks, annotation guidelines, and evaluation code.

title: ClosureBench: A Benchmark for Reasoning under Closure Assumptions
summary: AI agents built on large language models (LLMs) often answer questions from incomplete records. Missing information might be interpreted as unknown or false, depending on the completeness of the source. Current evaluations fail to distinguish these two aspects, as they are usually interwoven with other reasoning demands. We present ClosureBench, a benchmark that tests whether LLMs follow the stated rules for dealing with missing information. Every base scenario is tested under OWA, CWA, and LCWA, and only the treatment of missing information changes between variants. ClosureBench provides a verified base benchmark as well as agent extensions for action choice, source scope, and updates. A model is considered correct on a base scenario only if it provides correct answers in all of its closure variants. Across 960 instances, overall accuracy can mask substantial closure mistakes. Models achieve overall accuracy from 71.18% to 99.86% across replicated runs, but their core switch accuracy, measured on the scenarios whose gold label actually changes with the contract, varies between 18.23% and 99.31%. Large discrepancies emerge under LCWA. For example, some agents choose unknown despite the prompt indicating that missing information should be treated as false. Our findings demonstrate that evaluations of AI agents should not only measure whether agents can reason over existing facts but also whether they use the appropriate assumption when information is absent.

title: Rubric Semantics or Numerical Priors? Auditing Scale-Direction Bias in LLM Judges
summary: Recent benchmark evaluations increasingly rely on Large Language Models (LLMs) as automatic judges. This paradigm assumes LLMs evaluate based on the rubric's semantic meaning rather than its numeric scale. We question this assumption by introducing semantic faithfulness: the principle that semantically equivalent rubrics must yield consistent scores. To quantify this, we propose a scale-reversal probe that inverts score anchors without altering evaluation criteria. Furthermore, we introduce floor normalization to calibrate reversal disagreement against intrinsic model variability, enabling fair cross-model comparisons. Experiments across five meta-evaluation benchmarks with seven diverse LLM judges spanning open-weight and proprietary models reveal widespread violations of semantic faithfulness, showing that raw reversal agreement alone is misleading. Finally, we demonstrate that bidirectional anchor averaging reduces dependence on any single anchor direction without compromising alignment with human judgments. Our findings emphasize that trustworthy LLM judges must reliably follow rubric semantics, not just correlate with human ratings.

title: Your Software Factory Needs a Bill of Materials | Daniel Meppiel
summary:
Developers are about to write skills instead of code, and Microsoft's Daniel Meppiel argues the software factory that runs them needs versioning, a bill of materials and signed receipts before enterprises will trust it.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/7jw

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Simon Maple sits down with Daniel, of Microsoft's Global Black Belt team and creator of APM (Agent Package Manager), to dig into why teams keep rebuilding the same skills, how to version a skill when the change is in its behavior rather than a method signature, and why skills can only ever be guidance while security controls stay deterministic. Then stay for Daniel's full DevCon talk, Version Your Factory, Not Just Your Code, on agent contracts, signed receipts and the evidence a regulated enterprise needs before it auto-merges.

What we cover:
– Why developers will write skills and prose instead of code
– Why teams keep rebuilding the same skills, and the case for a shared skill catalog
– Testing and versioning skills with evals: when is a change a major version?
– APM, lock files and an agent bill of materials for your software factory
– Skills are guidance, security controls are deterministic
– Daniel's AI DevCon talk: agent contracts, signed receipts and auto-merging on evidence

title: From tasks to goals
summary: LangChain CEO and Co-founder Harrison Chase shares how we're moving from task-specific agents to goal-focused agents. Learn more.
content_excerpt: As agents become more powerful, we’re moving from giving them tasks to giving them goals. Under the hood, this move from tasks to goals consists of two more practical shifts: This is changes what an agent does, what it needs, how its built, and we interact with it. Previously, the user would specify tasks. Now, the user specifies a goal, and the agent iterates towards that goal by deconstructing into tasks, doing some of them, updating the task list, etc. The agent needs to be good at brainstorming and selecting different tasks, which requires new context engineering and prompting strategies. It needs to be somewhat creative - and varied - in brainstorming potential tasks (if it keeps on suggesting the same tasks over and over again, that’s not great). Practical consideration: you need some way to see what tasks the agent is doing (e.g. a to-do list), as well as prompting for the agent to be creative in coming up with tasks When you give an agent task, you largely have an idea of what tools it will call. When you give it a goal - you don’t really know what tools it will call, and you may not even know what tools it will need to call. Practical consideration: you need more controls over what tools an agent can or cannot call When you give an agent a task, you’re naturally in the loop. If you don’t provide all the information up front, its easy for the agent to ask follow up questions in chat. When you give an agent a goal - it may be running in the background and need to get clarification on certain points. It needs a way to ask questions to humans - whether through Slack or a dedicated UI. Practical consideration: you need a mechanism for a background agent to ask you for clarification The agent needs to know how its doing as it progresses towards a goal. This could either be by checking in on a metric to see if it is improving, or by getting explicit feedback from a human on how its doing. The more closely tied to a metric, the better in some sense (easy for it to track automatically!) but its never wise to blindly optimize a metric, so explicit human feedback may be the best thing. This is why its important to design goals in a way where its easy to give feedback. You can have both metrics for the agent to drive towards, and a way to get feedback from users. title: claude-code v2.1.329
summary:
What's changed

  • Added a trust dialog warning that says where a folder's hooks are declared
  • Added a warning in the conversation, in Claude Desktop and other non-interactive hosts, when hooks in managed settings fail to load
  • Added this session's scheduled tasks, /loop wakeups, the goal and this conversation's forks to /tasks; x stops one after asking

  • Added support for turning on Code Mode while OpenTelemetry events and metrics are enabled; each tool call the code makes sends its events; tracing still keeps it off
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json sometimes being reset to defaults when a network stall or file lock made it unreadable and cleared during a save
  • Fixed repeated sign-outs on macOS when Claude Code could read the Keychain but not save to it. That session now stops at expiry and says why, and other sessions stay signed in
  • Fixed /terminal-setup corrupting VS Code settings or keybindings files around block comments, and reporting success while losing the Shift+Enter binding where keybindings.json has an unclosed string
  • Fixed files accepted through the IDE diff being saved without their last newline, and losing their byte order mark (BOM) when an edit was accepted by saving the diff in VS Code
  • Fixed picking a cloud session in /teleport replacing your open conversation: the pick now starts a new session, as /clear does, and /resume brings the old one back
  • Fixed /usage-credits asking Pro and Max users to log in again after opening the browser, and the link disappearing after 8 seconds if the browser doesn't open and a task stops for usage credits
  • Fixed /usage saying usage credits are off when they had run out or reached the monthly limit, and /model not telling Pro and Max users when that limit blocks a model that runs on usage credits
  • Fixed the spend limit menu showing your spend as your monthly limit and wrapping its rows under the pointer in narrow windows
  • Fixed a status line script that prints without end freezing the prompt and using gigabytes of memory
  • Fixed an empty, frozen screen after approving managed settings while the --resume picker, the trust dialog or another set-up screen was waiting
  • Fixed choosing Default in /model replacing your saved model with your organization's default when the Default row already showed your saved model
  • Fixed an MCP server being signed in again after you cleared its authentication while a token refresh was running
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stalled after a slow reconnect: Claude Code now reconnects most HTTP MCP servers by itself when one is left on an older protocol version

  • Fixed /code-review <pr number> sometimes reviewing the checked-out branch instead of the pull request without saying so: it now reads the pull request with gh pr diff, or says when it can't
  • Fixed /code-review stopping at a permission prompt, on most models, to look for a ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md that doesn't exist
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --push-outcome-on-release sometimes deleting a session's branch on the git host
  • Fixed Code Mode hiding a script's finished edits and the stopped command after Esc, and losing them on exit

title: Same Judgement, Different Scores: Numerical Scoring Topology in LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluation
summary: LLMs are increasingly used as automated evaluators to reduce the cost and time required for human annotation. However, the role of scoring-scheme design in the reliability of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation remains underexplored. To address this problem, we introduce numerical scoring topology, which characterizes the structural design of a scoring scheme in terms of its scale width, granularity, offset, symmetry, and boundary placement. Building on this definition, we conduct the first systematic study of how numerical scoring topology influences zero-shot LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation across diverse benchmarks and judge models. Our results show that numerical scoring topology systematically affects judge scores, calibration, and robustness, particularly in judgment-intensive evaluations. Shifted and narrow ranges tend to induce some of the largest score deviations across many settings. We further find that stronger and larger judge models generally achieve higher discriminative validity and greater robustness to scoring-topology changes. These findings suggest that numerical scoring topology should be treated as an integral component of LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation and highlight the need for more principled and standardized scoring protocols.

title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
